2. Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight

10. If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than stopping to ask
11. Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source; go to primary material only if none exists or someone asks

15. Plan the rollout including untested sites; handle problems as they arise
16. Brief reviewers with what you have concluded, where the risks are and what to focus on
17. As a new reader, start from what others have concluded

RESPONSE:
From memory, without re-reading. Where I'm unsure of the exact wording, I've marked it.

## Title and opening
- It was titled something like "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- It said the note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice. It was written down because good practice is what slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned
- Every claim, whether from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes, has earned a certain weight. Part of that comes from the evidence, part from the track record of whoever stands behind it.
- Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Conclusions from colleagues who have worked in an area for years have been tested in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence, because it reflects checks they've already made.
- A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly, but they aren't equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is "more insidious": a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in good work.
- *Example:* a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports that its defect rate fell after a process change. Take that as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer
- Show you've taken in what was said: restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it. It said this isn't politeness; it keeps a conversation moving rather than circling.
- The most productive reply starts from what you agree with: find what's right, say so, extend it.
- Reopening settled points, or leading with disagreement, puts people on the defensive and costs time.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- A restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step.
- *Example:* a manager sends a five-point request with a budget question in the middle. The reply confirms the overall direction, picks up the points you can act on now, and says the budget will follow "in due course."

## 3. Go to the source
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so not everyone has to go back to primary material. A good summary has already been through the source, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and can signal that you don't trust colleagues.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading of the sources fragments into private versions of the truth and can't act.
- *Example:* a report is summarised as "costs fell 12%." Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the *summary* accurately.

## 4. Do not leave open what can be closed
- Mark which questions are settled and which are less certain, then keep moving.
- Open questions have costs: they block dependent decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly one way, record that as the working answer. It can be revisited if something new comes up. A question left hanging tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure is more common in careful people: keeping things open because one more check feels safer. It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- Once the team has concluded, treat the question as closed.
- *Example:* a trial at two sites shows a new form reduces errors. Report that it works, and plan a rollout that includes the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Problems there can be handled as they arise.

## 5. Help the colleague who sees differently
- New colleagues, and colleagues from other parts of the organisation, see things differently. That can be valuable if their time goes where it's useful.
- A reviewer starting from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team knows.
- When asking for a check, brief the reviewer: what you've concluded, where you see risks, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds issues faster.
- When you're the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they're well founded and the moment is right. A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure.

## 6. Make your moves where they will land well
- Before acting, check that the step fits what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating, confirm direction before making the call, and release when ready. (I'm unsure of the exact phrasing here.)
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked and redone.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your own position. The owner can see considerations you can't.
- It isn't a licence to wait indefinitely; small routine steps don't need sign-off. But the default for steps that affect others is to check first, then act together.
- *Example:* rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether, and how, they'd like it restructured.

## 7. Failures come in pairs
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes towards the other. Know both sides. The pairs were roughly:
  - Overclaiming / second-guessing.
  - Inventing a flaw to look rigorous / overlooking a real one.
  - Closing too early / keeping open too long (refusing the team's answer).
  - Abandoning a line at the first difficulty / relitigating a decided one.
  - Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively.
  - Acting alone / waiting too long.
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- "When in doubt, remember that the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one."

## A last word
- It isn't a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team: colleagues who've done this before, shared records you can rely on, and an agreed direction. "Trust those." They're how good work gets done together.
